title: From the heart (Mark 7:1–23)
hookLine: it's what comes out of the heart that makes unclean

cards: The kitchen gets cleaned when guests are coming. The outside is the easy part.
Then there's what comes out when nobody's performing: the comment under your breath in traffic, the text you send when you're angry, what you say about someone once they've left the room.
Today, an argument about clean hands turns into a teaching about exactly that.

teach.b: First, the washing. Some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and notice that some of Jesus's disciples eat bread without washing their hands in the ritual way.
Mark explains the custom: the Pharisees, holding the tradition of the elders, washed their hands before eating, and washed cups and pots too. This wasn't about germs.

Some scholars explain it as a practice of holiness, bringing something of the Temple's purity to an ordinary table. A ritual handwashing with a blessing before bread is still part of Jewish practice today.

Jesus answers with Isaiah: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." His example: a man declares his goods corban, a gift set aside for God, and so does nothing for his father or mother.
The rule is kept; the parents get nothing.
Third, the saying, to the crowd: "There is nothing from without a man that entering into him, can defile him. But the things which come from a man, those are they that defile a man."

teach.h: WHAT COMES OUT OF THE HEART.
teach.b: Later, alone with the disciples, he explains: "For from within out of the heart of men proceed evil thoughts", and the list goes on: murders, thefts, covetousness, deceit, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride.

teach.h: THEIR HEART IS FAR FROM ME.
teach.b: Mark adds a short aside, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "purging all meats"; some translations take it to mean Jesus made all foods clean, and Christians came to eat any food.
Observant Jews continue to keep the food laws as God's commandments, and hear this debate as one among teachers.
Catholics hear its center in the saying itself: in Mark's telling, what defiles a person starts on the inside.

how: Catholics hear this gospel at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the daily examination of conscience, reviewing words and actions and the heart behind them, is a Catholic practice.

o: just the feelings, apart from the mind
the blood-pumping organ in your chest
the center of thought, will and feeling

games.q: what's inside the reading — tap the pairs.
p: money set aside, parents left unfed

s: the handwashing in this story was about hygiene
it was a practice of holiness, often explained as bringing something of the Temple's purity to the ordinary table.
ritual handwashing with a blessing before bread is still Jewish practice
a practice of holiness kept in Jewish homes today.
Jesus says nothing going into a person can defile them
what defiles comes out of the heart: evil thoughts, thefts, deceit, an evil eye, pride.

games.q: a man says his money is set apart for God, so he does nothing for his father or mother. the rule is kept. what does Jesus say?
o: you've set aside God's commandment to keep your tradition.
games.why: Jesus uses corban as his example of honoring God with the lips while the heart is far away. the parents get nothing.

practice: Think back over yesterday: not what you planned to say, but what actually came out of you, a kind word, a sharp one, something said behind someone's back.
Don't argue with yourself; just look, then look underneath: was your heart tired, hurt, afraid? If you pray, offer your heart to God as it is, and ask for a clean one; if you don't, just notice.

wordCard.voice: Heart. Not just emotion, but the center of thought, will and feeling, where what defiles a person starts. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: heart, in the Bible the center of thought, will and feeling, not only emotion.

carryVoice: Your line: out of the heart. Seven days: Legion, two daughters, the carpenter, the twelve, rest, the rowers, and now the heart. Day two hundred ten, in the book.
